title: Shortest Distance to a Character
statement: You are given a string `s` and a single letter `c` that is guaranteed to appear in `s` at least once. Build an integer array `answer` of the same length as `s`, where `answer[i]` is the smallest value of `|i - j|` over all indices `j` with `s[j] == c`. Return `answer`.
constraints: s[i] and c are lowercase English letters
c appears in s at least once
notes:
## Intuition

For each index the closest `c` is either the nearest one on its left or the nearest one on its right. The brute force scans the whole string for every index, which is O(n²). Instead, walk `i` from left to right while a second pointer, `next`, always sits on the first `c` at or after `i`, and `prev` remembers the last `c` already passed. Both pointers only move forward, so the whole scan is linear.

## Approach

1. Move `next` to the first `c` in `s` (one exists). `prev = -1` means no `c` seen yet.
2. For each `i`: when `i` reaches `next`, this `c` becomes `prev`, and `next` moves on to the following `c` (or to `n` if there is none).
3. Compute `toPrev = i - prev` and `toNext = next - i`, using `Infinity` for a side with no `c`.
4. Store the smaller one in `answer[i]`.

## Example 1, step by step

`s = "loveleetcode"`, `c = "e"`, so the `e`s are at 3, 5, 6 and 11. `next` starts at 3; indices 0, 1, 2 have only a right side: 3, 2, 1. At `i = 3`, `prev = 3` and `next` moves to 5, giving 0, then `i = 4` gets min(1, 1) = 1. At 5 and 6 the answer is 0 (`next` moves to 6, then 11). Indices 7 to 10 get min(1, 4), min(2, 3), min(3, 2), min(4, 1), i.e. 1, 2, 2, 1, and index 11 gets 0: `[3,2,1,0,1,0,0,1,2,2,1,0]`.

## Complexity

- Time: O(n): `i` and `next` each cross the string once.
- Space: O(1) besides the returned array.

## Pitfalls

- Before the first `c` there is no left neighbour, and after the last one there is no right neighbour; use `Infinity` there, not a distance to index `-1` or `n`.
- Looking only to the left (or only to the right) gives wrong answers on half of the string.
- Advance `next` past the current `i` when `s[i] === c`, or the next index would still measure to an old position.

## Variables

| Name | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `n` | length of `s` |
| `answer` | the distances being built |
| `prev` | index of the last `c` at or before `i`, or `-1` |
| `next` | index of the nearest `c` to the right of `prev`, or `n` when none is left |
| `toPrev`, `toNext` | distance from `i` to `prev` and to `next` |

narration.4: No c has been passed yet, so there is no left neighbour.
narration.5: next will point at the first c in the string.
narration.6: Walk next forward until it lands on c; one is guaranteed to exist.
narration.9: Visit every index from left to right.
narration.10: i has reached the c that next points at.
narration.11: That c now becomes the nearest one on the left.
narration.13: Move next forward to the following c, or to n if there is none.
narration.17: Distance to the nearest c on the left, or Infinity if there is none.
narration.18: Distance to the nearest c on the right, or Infinity if there is none.
narration.19: The closer of the two sides is the answer for i.
narration.21: Every index now holds its shortest distance.
